name: Baseline
definition: The invisible line that most letters sit on, and the line every other vertical type metric is measured from.
useWhen: aligning text with an icon or another line of text
notes: Anchor term for the whole metrics cluster.

name: X-height
definition: The height of a lowercase x in a typeface, measured from the baseline, which is what makes two fonts at the same point size look different sizes.
useWhen: explaining why two fonts at the same size look different

name: Cap height
definition: The height of a capital letter measured from the baseline, and the edge designers usually mean when they say text should line up flush.
useWhen: aligning a heading optically instead of by its box

name: Ascender
definition: The part of a lowercase letter such as b, d, or h that rises above the x-height.
useWhen: naming the strokes that reach above lowercase height

name: Descender
definition: The part of a letter such as g, j, p, or y that drops below the baseline.
useWhen: naming the strokes that hang below the baseline

name: Counter
definition: The fully enclosed white space inside a letter such as o, b, or the upper bowl of an a.
useWhen: describing the hole inside a letterform

name: Aperture
definition: The partly enclosed opening in a letter such as the gap at the bottom of a lowercase e or the mouth of a c.
useWhen: explaining why one sans feels more legible at small sizes

name: Overshoot
definition: The tiny amount by which round and pointed letters extend past the baseline or cap line so they look the same size as flat ones.
useWhen: explaining why a circle must be drawn larger than a square
notes: Same optical-correction idea an icon designer applies to circular glyphs; possible seeAlso into an icon term.

name: Ink trap
definition: A notch cut out of a letter's inside corners so spreading ink or blurring pixels do not fill the joint solid.
useWhen: naming the cut-out notches in a display typeface

name: Tittle
definition: The dot above a lowercase i or j.
useWhen: you need the word for the dot on an i

name: Half-leading
definition: The empty space a browser splits evenly above and below a line of text when line height exceeds the font's own height, which is why text boxes never sit flush.
useWhen: explaining the mystery padding around a line of text

sources.title: Leading-Trim: The Future of Digital Typesetting

name: Text box trim
definition: Cutting the leftover space above and below a line of text so the box hugs the cap height and baseline instead of the font's full ascent and descent.
useWhen: you want a label's box to match the letters, not the font
notes: Strong tail term; the property was renamed from leading-trim, so both spellings are live search queries.

name: Typeface
definition: The designed set of letterforms itself, as distinct from a font, which is one particular file or instance you actually use.
useWhen: distinguishing the design from the file

sources.title: Family, type family, or font family (Google Fonts Knowledge)

notes: Typeface vs font is the classic disambiguation entry; keep them as one term with the other as an alias.

name: Glyph
definition: A single drawn shape in a font, which may be one character, a variant of one, or several characters fused together.
useWhen: talking about drawn shapes rather than characters

name: Serif
definition: The small finishing stroke at the end of a letter's stem, and by extension the class of typefaces that have them.
useWhen: naming the little feet on the ends of strokes

name: Sans-serif
definition: A typeface drawn without finishing strokes on the ends of its stems, which is the default register of most interface type.
useWhen: naming type without finishing strokes
notes: Classification families (grotesque, neo-grotesque, humanist, geometric, slab) are a possible sub-cluster if the taxonomy wants them.

name: Monospace
definition: A typeface in which every character occupies the same horizontal width, so characters stack into columns down the page.
useWhen: code, terminals, or anything that must line up in columns

name: Superfamily
definition: A type system whose serif, sans, and sometimes mono members share one skeleton, so they pair by construction rather than by taste.
useWhen: picking two typefaces that are guaranteed to agree

name: Font pairing
definition: Choosing two or more typefaces that work together, usually one expressive and one neutral, with enough contrast to read as a deliberate choice.
useWhen: deciding which two typefaces to run together

sources.title: Three secrets to font pairing (Adobe Design)

name: Type specimen
definition: A display of a typeface's characters, sizes, and styles made to show what the face can do rather than to communicate the text itself.
useWhen: showing off a typeface rather than using it

name: Pangram
definition: A sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once, used to show a whole character set in one line.
useWhen: you need one line that shows every letter

name: Lorem ipsum
definition: Scrambled pseudo-Latin placeholder text used so a layout can be judged on its shape and texture before the real copy exists.
useWhen: filling a layout before the copy is written
notes: Greeking is the broader practice; lorem ipsum is the specific text and the far more common search query.

name: Type scale
definition: The fixed set of text sizes a design allows, chosen so sizes relate to each other rather than being picked one at a time.
useWhen: deciding what sizes are allowed to exist at all

name: Modular scale
definition: A type scale generated by multiplying a base size by a fixed ratio, so every step is proportionally related to the one before it.
useWhen: generating sizes from a ratio instead of picking them

sources.title: What the Font are Vertical Rhythm and Modular Scale?

name: Fluid typography
definition: Type sizes that scale continuously with the viewport between a minimum and a maximum, rather than jumping at breakpoints.
useWhen: sizing text across screens without breakpoints

sources.title: Creating a Fluid Type Scale (Modern CSS)

name: Typographic hierarchy
definition: The ordering of text by visual weight so a reader can tell at a glance what is a title, what is body, and what is a caption.
useWhen: making importance readable without reading

implementations.name: Type roles: display, headline, title, body, label

name: Typography token
definition: A named bundle of type values (family, size, weight, line height, tracking) that a design system hands out instead of raw numbers.
useWhen: naming a text style so it can be reused and themed
notes: Sits at the border of typography and a future design-token cluster; merge candidate with any generic design-token entry.

name: Baseline grid
definition: A repeating horizontal grid that every line of text sits on, so text in separate columns or cards lines up across the layout.
useWhen: making text in separate columns line up across a page

implementations.name: Line heights aligned to the 4px grid

notes: Could arguably be category layout; kept in typography because the grid unit is the line of text.

name: Vertical rhythm
definition: Spacing every block of text by multiples of one line height so the page keeps an even beat from top to bottom.
useWhen: spacing paragraphs and headings by one consistent unit

sources.title: What the Font are Vertical Rhythm and Modular Scale?

name: Point size
definition: The nominal size of type, measured in points, which describes the body the letters are drawn on rather than the height of any letter.
useWhen: explaining why 16pt in two fonts looks different

name: Em
definition: A relative unit equal to the current font size, historically the width of the square the letter m was cast on.
useWhen: sizing something relative to the text it sits in
notes: rem is close enough that it may deserve its own entry during canonicalize.

name: Ch unit
definition: A CSS length equal to the advance width of the digit zero in the current font, used to set column widths in characters rather than pixels.
useWhen: setting a column width in characters, not pixels

name: Measure
definition: The width of a column of text, judged in characters per line, with roughly 45 to 75 treated as the comfortable range for reading.
useWhen: deciding how wide a paragraph is allowed to get

sources.title: Choose a comfortable measure (Elements of Typographic Style Applied to the Web)

name: Rag
definition: The uneven edge left by unjustified text, and the thing typographers tune so that edge makes no distracting shapes down the side of a paragraph.
useWhen: critiquing the uneven edge of a paragraph

name: River
definition: An accidental channel of white space running down a paragraph where word spaces on consecutive lines happen to line up.
useWhen: naming the white streak running down a paragraph

name: Widow
definition: A short last line of a paragraph, often a single word, stranded at the top of the next column or page.
useWhen: naming a stranded last line at the top of a column

sources.title: An end to typographic widows on the web (Clagnut)

notes: Widow and orphan are defined in opposite directions by different sources; the entry has to say so.

name: Orphan
definition: A first line of a paragraph left alone at the bottom of a column or page, with the rest of the paragraph carried over.
useWhen: naming a first line left behind at the bottom of a column

name: Runt
definition: A single word left alone on the last line of a paragraph or heading.
useWhen: naming the lone word on a heading's last line

sources.title: An end to typographic widows on the web (Clagnut)

notes: Casually called a widow by most web designers; strong disambiguation entry against widow and orphan.

name: Justified text
definition: Text set so both edges of the column are flush, achieved by stretching or squeezing the spaces between words on each line.
useWhen: you want both edges of a column flush

name: Hyphenation
definition: Breaking a word across two lines at a syllable boundary so lines fill more evenly, marked with a hyphen at the break.
useWhen: keeping narrow columns from tearing open

name: Hyphenation ladder
definition: Three or more consecutive lines ending in a hyphen, which builds a visible staircase down the right edge of a column.
useWhen: naming a stack of hyphens down a column edge

name: Hanging punctuation
definition: Letting quotes, hyphens, and other light marks sit outside the text column so the edge of the text reads as straight to the eye.
useWhen: a quote mark makes the left edge look dented

sources.title: Hung Punctuation and Optical Margin Alignment (CreativePro)

notes: Merge candidate: optical margin alignment is InDesign's name for the same effect and should stay an alias, not a term.

name: Text balancing
definition: Choosing line breaks so a short block of text has lines of roughly equal length instead of a long first line and a stub second one.
useWhen: a two line heading breaks badly

sources.title: When to use text-wrap: balance vs pretty (LogRocket)

notes: balance and pretty solve different problems (even lines vs no stranded last word); canonicalize may want to split them.

name: First-line indent
definition: Indenting the opening line of a paragraph so the start of each paragraph is visible without a blank line between them.
useWhen: marking new paragraphs without adding space

name: Hanging indent
definition: A paragraph whose first line starts further left than the rest, so the following lines are indented under it.
useWhen: setting bibliographies, definitions, or list labels

name: Typographic color
definition: The overall lightness or darkness a block of text produces when you stop reading it and look at it as a grey texture.
useWhen: judging a paragraph as texture rather than words
notes: Cross-category trap: the word color here has nothing to do with the color category. Worth a contrastWith into semantic-color.

name: Word spacing
definition: The width of the gaps between words, which justification stretches and which, set too wide, opens rivers down a paragraph.
useWhen: the gaps between words, not between letters

name: Optical kerning
definition: Letting software space letter pairs by looking at their shapes, instead of using the pair values the type designer built into the font.
useWhen: a font's own spacing is unreliable at display size
notes: Kerning already exists on the site; this is the metric vs optical distinction, which is a separate question and a separate search.

name: Drop cap
definition: An oversized opening letter set into the first lines of a paragraph, marking where the reading starts.
useWhen: marking where an article begins

sources.title: How to Use Drop Caps effectively

name: Raised cap
definition: An oversized opening letter that sits on the first line's baseline and rises above the text, rather than sinking into it.
useWhen: the big opening letter rises instead of sinking
notes: relatedSlugs mentions initial-letter, which is currently an alias of drop-cap rather than a term; resolve in canonicalize.

name: Pull quote
definition: A phrase lifted out of an article and set large as a graphic element, to draw a browsing reader into the text.
useWhen: advertising a line of the article to a scanner

sources.title: How to Attract Attention With Pull Quotes (CreativePro)

name: Eyebrow
definition: A short line of text above a heading that says what category or series the content belongs to.
useWhen: labelling what kind of thing a heading is
notes: Material's older overline style is the closest design-system equivalent; kept as an alias.

name: Deck
definition: The short summary line set between a headline and the body, larger than body text and written to sell the article.
useWhen: the summary line under a headline

name: Small caps
definition: Capital letters drawn at roughly lowercase height, with weight adjusted to match, so an abbreviation does not shout inside running text.
useWhen: setting acronyms inside body text without shouting

name: Petite caps
definition: Capitals drawn to exactly x-height, shorter than small caps, so they sit flush with the lowercase around them.
useWhen: you need caps that match x-height exactly

name: All caps
definition: Text set entirely in capitals, which reads slower than mixed case because the word's outline shape disappears.
useWhen: short labels that must shout, never sentences

sources.title: Title case vs sentence case in UI

name: Title case
definition: Capitalizing the first letter of each significant word in a heading or label, leaving short articles and prepositions lowercase.
useWhen: Apple-style headings, buttons, and menu labels

name: Sentence case
definition: Capitalizing only the first word of a label or heading, plus any proper nouns, as you would in an ordinary sentence.
useWhen: Google-style UI copy and anything meant to be read

sources.title: Title case vs sentence case in UI

name: Italic
definition: A companion style with letterforms redrawn on a cursive model, not merely slanted, used for emphasis and titles.
useWhen: emphasis inside running text

name: Oblique
definition: An upright typeface slanted to the right without redrawing its letters, which is why it lacks the cursive forms a true italic has.
useWhen: distinguishing a slanted roman from a real italic

name: Faux bold
definition: A bold or italic the browser fakes by smearing or shearing the regular weight, because the real style was never loaded.
useWhen: your bold looks wrong and blurry

name: Font weight
definition: How thick a typeface's strokes are, named in steps from thin to black and numbered from 100 to 900 on the web.
useWhen: naming how heavy the strokes are

name: Tabular figures
definition: Numerals drawn to identical widths so digits stack into columns, and so a changing number does not shift the text around it.
useWhen: numbers in a table, a timer, or a live counter

sources.title: OpenType at Work: Figure Styles (Type Network)

notes: Proportional figures are the contrasting setting; worth an alias row or its own stub.

name: Oldstyle figures
definition: Numerals with varying heights, some rising and some dropping below the baseline, so numbers blend into lowercase running text.
useWhen: numbers inside a sentence, not in a table

sources.title: OpenType at Work: Figure Styles (Type Network)

name: Lining figures
definition: Numerals all drawn to cap height so they line up evenly with capitals and with each other.
useWhen: numbers next to capitals or in interface chrome

sources.title: OpenType at Work: Figure Styles (Type Network)

name: Ligature
definition: A single glyph that replaces two or more letters whose shapes would otherwise collide, such as the f and i pair.
useWhen: two letters collide and the font fuses them
notes: Discretionary ligatures folded in as an alias rather than split out; revisit if the demo wants to show both.

name: Contextual alternates
definition: Substitute letterforms a font swaps in automatically based on the neighbouring characters, so joins and repeats look natural.
useWhen: a script font changes shape depending on its neighbours

sources.title: Syntax for OpenType features in CSS (Adobe Fonts)

name: Stylistic set
definition: A numbered bundle of alternate glyphs inside a font, switched on as a group to change the look of certain letters.
useWhen: switching a font's single-storey a on

sources.title: Syntax for OpenType features in CSS (Adobe Fonts)
A Practical Guide to Alternate Characters (Pangram Pangram)

name: Swash
definition: A letter drawn with an ornamental flourish, usually an extended entry or exit stroke on an italic capital.
useWhen: naming the decorative tail on a fancy capital

name: OpenType features
definition: Optional glyph substitutions and spacing rules packed inside a font file, addressed by four-letter tags and switched on from CSS.
useWhen: reaching for a font capability that is off by default

name: Superscript
definition: Small raised characters used for footnote markers, ordinals, and exponents, ideally drawn by the font rather than shrunk by software.
useWhen: footnote markers, ordinals, and exponents

name: Variable font
definition: One font file that contains a continuous design space, so any weight, width, or other axis value between the extremes can be requested.
useWhen: you need many weights without many files

name: Variation axis
definition: One dimension a variable font can move along, named by a four-letter tag: lowercase for the five registered axes, uppercase for custom ones.
useWhen: naming a single dial inside a variable font

name: Optical size
definition: A font adjusting its own drawing for the size it is set at, thickening strokes and opening spacing for small text and refining both for large.
useWhen: type that should be redrawn, not just scaled

implementations.name: SF Pro Text and SF Pro Display switching

name: Grade
definition: A variable font axis that thickens or thins strokes without changing any character's width, so text can get darker without reflowing.
useWhen: darkening text on a dark background without reflow

name: Named instance
definition: A specific point in a variable font's design space that the designer has given a style name, so it can be picked like an ordinary weight.
useWhen: picking a named style out of a variable font

name: Web font
definition: A font file downloaded by the page rather than taken from the reader's device, declared in CSS and delivered like any other asset.
useWhen: type the page ships rather than borrows

name: Font stack
definition: The ordered list of typefaces a rule names, each tried in turn until one is available, ending in a generic family.
useWhen: listing which fonts to try and in what order

sources.title: Creating Perfect Font Fallbacks in CSS

name: Fallback font
definition: The typeface actually used when the preferred one is missing or has not loaded, either for the whole run of text or for characters it lacks.
useWhen: naming what shows up when the real font does not

sources.title: Framework tools for font fallbacks (Chrome for Developers)
Creating Perfect Font Fallbacks in CSS

name: System font
definition: The typeface the operating system uses for its own interface, requested by keyword so each platform supplies its native face.
useWhen: you want the app to look native and load nothing

name: FOUT
definition: The visible swap when a page first paints text in a fallback face and then re-renders it once the web font arrives.
useWhen: the text visibly changes font on load

name: FOIT
definition: The blank period when a browser hides text entirely rather than show it in a fallback face while the web font loads.
useWhen: the text is missing, not just wrong, on load

sources.title: Ensure text remains visible during webfont load (Lighthouse)

name: FOFT
definition: A loading strategy that shows the roman weight as soon as it arrives and lets the remaining styles swap in afterwards, so the swap happens in stages.
useWhen: staging a font swap instead of taking it all at once

name: Font metric override
definition: Reshaping a fallback font's size and vertical metrics in CSS so it occupies the same space as the web font and the swap shifts nothing.
useWhen: killing the layout jump when a web font lands

sources.title: Framework tools for font fallbacks (Chrome for Developers)
Creating Perfect Font Fallbacks in CSS

notes: Sits between typography and performance; the layout-shift angle may pull it toward a future performance cluster.

name: Font subsetting
definition: Shipping only the characters a page actually needs, cutting the font file down and letting the browser fetch ranges on demand.
useWhen: cutting a font file down to what the page uses

name: Tofu
definition: The empty rectangle a font renders when it has no glyph for a character, named for the block of bean curd it resembles.
useWhen: naming the empty box where a character should be

name: Hinting
definition: Instructions inside a font that nudge its outlines onto the pixel grid at small sizes so stems stay crisp and even.
useWhen: explaining why type looks fuzzy at small sizes

name: Font smoothing
definition: How a device softens the edges of letterforms, either by shading whole pixels grey or by lighting a pixel's coloured subpixels separately.
useWhen: your type looks heavier on one platform than another

sources.title: What's the deal with WebKit Font Smoothing?

name: Truncation
definition: Cutting text that does not fit and marking the cut, usually with an ellipsis, so the reader knows something was removed.
useWhen: text has to fit a box it does not fit

name: Line clamp
definition: Cutting a block of text off after a fixed number of lines, with an ellipsis at the end of the last one.
useWhen: capping a card's description at three lines

name: Word break
definition: Whether a long unbroken string is allowed to split mid-word rather than overflow its container, and where that split may happen.
useWhen: a long URL or token is bursting out of its box

name: Soft hyphen
definition: An invisible character placed inside a word that marks where a hyphen may appear if the word has to break, and stays hidden otherwise.
useWhen: telling the browser where a long word may break

name: Non-breaking space
definition: A space that renders normally but forbids a line break, gluing two words together so they never end up on separate lines.
useWhen: keeping a number and its unit on one line

name: Zero-width space
definition: An invisible character that takes no width and adds a legal break point, letting a long string wrap without showing a hyphen.
useWhen: breaking a long identifier with no visible mark

name: Smart quotes
definition: The curved opening and closing quotation marks a typeface actually draws, as opposed to the straight vertical marks inherited from typewriters.
useWhen: your quotes look like typewriter ticks

sources.title: The Definitive Guide to Quotes, Apostrophes, and Primes

name: Prime mark
definition: The slanted tick used for feet, inches, minutes, and seconds, which is a different character from either a straight quote or a curly one.
useWhen: writing feet and inches, not quoting anyone

name: Em dash
definition: The longest common dash, about the width of the letter m, used to set off an abrupt break or aside in a sentence.
useWhen: naming the longest dash on the keyboard
notes: Awkward but necessary: the site bans the character in its own prose (SPEC 2.4) while still owing readers the definition. Author with care.

name: En dash
definition: A dash about the width of the letter n, used for ranges of numbers and for connections between two things.
useWhen: writing a range of numbers or dates

name: Pilcrow
definition: The paragraph mark, a reversed P with a doubled stem, used to show where a paragraph begins or as a hover anchor beside a heading.
useWhen: naming the paragraph symbol in an editor

name: Underline
definition: A rule drawn under text, on the web the default marker for a link, ideally set to skip the descenders it would otherwise cross.
useWhen: marking a link without relying on color alone

name: Strikethrough
definition: A rule drawn through the middle of text to mark it as removed, superseded, or no longer the current price.
useWhen: showing text that no longer applies

name: Ruby annotation
definition: Small guide text set beside or above a run of base text, most often to give the pronunciation of East Asian characters.
useWhen: annotating characters with their pronunciation

name: Bidirectional text
definition: Text mixing a right-to-left script with left-to-right runs such as numbers or Latin words, where each run keeps its own direction.
useWhen: Arabic or Hebrew text containing Latin or digits
notes: Arguably layout or accessibility; recorded as typography because the subject is how text sets.

name: Vertical writing mode
definition: Setting lines to run top to bottom in columns rather than left to right, as traditional Chinese, Japanese, and Korean typography does.
useWhen: typesetting CJK text in columns

name: Legibility
definition: How easily one letter can be told apart from another, a property of the typeface's drawing rather than of how the text is set.
useWhen: judging the typeface, not the setting

name: Readability
definition: How comfortably a body of text can be read at length, a property of the setting: size, measure, leading, and contrast.
useWhen: judging the setting, not the typeface
notes: Legibility and readability are the classic mixed-up pair; they should contrastWith each other.

name: Dynamic Type
definition: A platform feature that scales interface text to a size the reader chose in system settings, with layouts expected to reflow around it.
useWhen: the reader, not the designer, picks the text size
notes: Cross-category: equally an accessibility term. Recorded as typography since the subject is type sizing.

name: Text spacing
definition: The requirement that a reader can increase line height, letter spacing, word spacing, and paragraph spacing without any content being lost or clipped.
useWhen: proving a layout survives reader-set spacing
notes: CROSS-CATEGORY: filed under accessibility, surfaced by the typography sweep. Merge with the accessibility file's version if it enumerates one.

name: Icon font
definition: A font whose glyphs are icons rather than letters, addressed by code point or by a ligature so an icon can be styled like text.
useWhen: icons delivered as type instead of as images

sources.title: SVG, Icon Fonts, and Accessibility (24 Accessibility)

notes: Could equally be filed as component; the mechanism is a font, so typography.

name: Color font
definition: A font whose glyphs carry their own colors, gradients, or layers, with a palette the page can override rather than a single ink.
useWhen: type that carries its own colors

name: Emoji presentation
definition: Whether a character that can be either a symbol or an emoji renders as flat text or as a color emoji, selected by a variation selector or by CSS.
useWhen: a symbol turns into an emoji you did not want

name: Heading
definition: A short line of type that names the section under it and, by its size and weight, says how far down the outline that section sits.
useWhen: naming a section and showing its depth at once
notes: Round one caught heading-hierarchy (the outline rule) and typographic-hierarchy (the scale) but not the thing itself. The article should hold the two apart: level is semantic, size is a choice, and they are allowed to disagree.
